t: Does Teaching Students to Count Count as Much as Teaching Them What Counts? counts
q: But if you're not, I did want to share my take today on this idea that "teaching students to count" (academics) is not as important as "teaching them what counts.
Basically, it starts here: schools exist to promote the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them toward mastery of disciplines that they otherwise would be unlikely to master.
But when schools start thinking that this is their primary objective, they run the risk of deeply failing their students and all the while patting themselves on the back for doing so.

Cognitive scientists have basically settled the fact that the mind doesn't use knowledge as grist for the mill; instead, knowledge is the mill. We don't just think about what we know, we think with what we know.
If you don't, then students from homes where the disciplines and arts are valued will gain a significant advantage over students from homes where they are not.
But schools? These places MUST value an education in the disciplines and the arts. This is their unique role in society.
Teaching children to count — teaching them toward mastery of disciplines in school — is way better than fine. It's a sacred (and joyful) duty.

t: Who Knew We Were in Violent Agreement?
q: The extreme need to be right prevents people from listening to what others are saying — even when they are in agreement.
Parties who argue strongly against each other when they actually view the issue in the same way are said to be in violent agreement.
It speaks to a much deeper insecurity that will eventually undermine the leader’s ability to succeed with others.
Being right becomes a narcotic, easing the self-doubt and uncertainty they won’t admit to.
The more they insist on being right or more right, the more their credibility tumbles in the eyes of those who witness it.
Convincing someone who needs to be right that they are sometimes wrong is never fun. But it is the essential work of those who care.

t: How To Turn Your Classroom From Failure To Excellence
q: Although in the moment it doesn’t seem like a big deal, accepting less than what you ask of your students is a form of failure.
In fact, moving on in the face of any deviation from what you expect is inviting an accelerating decline of standards.
Nothing saves time more than well-done routines, transitions, activities, group and independent practices . . . you name it.
Reminders after misbehavior are always bad (enforce a consequence instead). Reminders before misbehavior can happen are good and most effective.
If in the rare case your students perform poorly after following the steps above, stop immediately, rewind back to the previous transition, and start again.
Once you develop the reputation for accepting only excellence, then that’s what you’ll get. Success begets success.
People naturally resist change and view it as uncomfortable, hard work, and time-consuming.
Instead of promoting the change, the best leaders co-create it with their team members.
Giving others the right to define the problem and its implications creates a sense of ownership that can’t be overstated.
Team members are left to grapple with the pace of making the change rather than the benefits or risks associated with it.
Once a change issue has been even half-baked without involvement from the team, resistance is sure to follow.
Trust the fact that the plane is much easier to land without the winds of discord blowing across the runway.

t: What I Talk About When I Talk to My Children about Spelling
q: I have no dreams of my children being top in their class or "exceptional" in any other way that the world measures. This is because I know what is true: that they are exceptional just as they are.

When they first started at the school, my daughters felt stressed about these lists and didn't do very well on them. When I learned of this, I told them not to fret and that we'd start to use our drive time to school to practice the lists.

Value: I try to emphasize to my children that it's fun to get better at spelling. I don't talk to them AT ALL about how they'll "use" spelling someday because I want them to see that education is about so much more than its utility.

As we've gone, they've both shifted from 50-60% on pretests to 80-95%, and I've taken care to gently point them toward how their consistent, simple effort — the car-ride testing — has led to these results.

Whenever I do sense them putting too much identification with the score, I push against that: "Woah, that test result seemed to really bug you. How come? … Well listen, it's just a test result. It's not you. You're great.
Leaders who have trouble remembering the names of those they meet have one of two issues.
They know that once a name is missed, it is exceptionally hard to recover from.
The truth is, unless a person’s short-term memory is significantly impaired, no one is bad at names.
Personal references, including names, invite people into a conversation. Not referring to them by name has the opposite effect.
The touchstone for mastering the skill is simply repeating the other person’s name immediately upon an introduction.
Launching into conversation does not burnish the name into memory, so a good leader must repeat it immediately.
In educational parlance, building community means to manufacture it.
You can’t force community. You can only set up conditions that nurture it. Otherwise, students will resist.
Tell a student they must say or write something nice about someone and they’ll do it, but if it’s not from the heart and of their own volition, then it’s hot air.
By far the most important and effective way to build community is to protect your students from bullying, name-calling, and disruption.
Competition builds new friendships, camaraderie, and community quickly and far better than a thousand kind letters.
So much is wasted on fluff and nonsense that take away from the one thing that helps students and their future more than anything else: Academics.
The idea of thinking in “first principles” was first discussed by Aristotle more than 2,000 years ago.
Leaders who adopt this approach essentially reverse engineer a problem.
Not surprisingly, most current solutions to problems are full of well-accepted assumptions that blind leaders from taking a different path.
Sticking to the facts but experimenting with the assumptions can sometimes yield an intriguing new dish.
First principles are the rules and causes that govern what you can and can’t do.
The deeper a leader digs into a problem using this type of thinking, the more fundamental truths and assumptions are exposed.
So much of effective teaching — and good living — comes down to how well you manage to stay atop the Yerkes-Dodson Curve.
On one side of the curve, you're burnt out and stretched thin. It's easy to get here because the work we do is important, which means there's tons of internal and external pressure sources.
But on the other side of the curve, you find yourself unchallenged, bored, and apathetic. You're disengaged; you're going through the motions.

If you're on the under-pressured side, you can do things like observe a colleague, read (and apply!) a new PD book, ask someone to sit in on your lessons, or set a challenge for yourself for the next month of your teaching.
And in all of it, don't get stressed about managing your stress. The last thing we want is to add pressure to our pressure because we feel pressure to make it perfect.

t: The True Purpose Of Classroom Management
q: The SCM approach to classroom management isn’t complicated. It isn’t burdensome or overbearing. It’s neither stressful nor manipulative.

It’s neither countdowns and threats and narrating students through every this and that. Nor is it a haphazard mix of “catching students doing good,” do-this-and-get-that economics, and other bribes, tricks, and manipulation.
What is the point of classroom management generally? Is it to force, subdue, and squeeze into a box?
It treats students like living and breathing people, respecting their intelligence and believing in their unlimited growth and capacity to overcome obstacles.
It’s to free the teacher to focus on great instruction and free the students to focus on their assignments and schoolwork responsibilities.

Walk into an SCM classroom and you won’t see obvious signs of classroom management. You’ll only notice the teacher, an expert in their content area, deep in the river of exacting and exuberant instruction.

t: The Teacher's Work Is Like the Landscape
q: I've taken a dozen or so walks these past couple of weeks because, when I'm in the valley, sometimes that's all I can do. Walking stabilizes my soul; it depressurizes me.

As I walked and felt the cold sinking in to me, I started seeing the landscape as it has appeared to me in other seasons. Beneath the ice and within the dormant plants there has been, and will be again, the first shoots of spring, the flourishing of summer, and the quiet, regalness of fall.

No matter how wintry your practice has felt this school year, colleague, reflect on how it has also housed the spring. Mastery has grown. Learning has taken place. And connection has done what connection does: alter life trajectories, for the better.
But, as a finite creature fixed in time, you may see none of it right now. We just don't get to see it all. Omniscience is not our place in the cosmos.
It's possible to see no results for months but still to be doing something important.

t: The Gist of a Gisty Book
q: In other words, it's a book that attempts to introduce a gist of good teaching, in any content area.

I made this book for teachers like me who are multivocational: we want to be excellent at our jobs for the sake of our students, but we're not willing to sacrifice our entire lives on the altar of teaching success.

There's no such thing as creating literate students who don't know a lot of things. Abilities that we prize in the twenty-first century, including the ability to learn, to read, and to think critically, are not transferrable to domains in which we have little knowledge.
If argument isn't situated in the context of a life-giving classroom culture, it's not going to promote the Key Beliefs we're after.
One needless cause of the literacy decline is a lack of reading volume in secondary schools. Each one of us can combat this without sacrificing content knowledge.

Speaking and listening are often neglected in our literacy teaching. These life-critical skills become the hapless victims of assumicide: because our students, for the most part, enter our classrooms speaking and listening, we assume that we don't need to give them instructions, practice, and feedback in these areas.

t: Sometimes a Team Just Needs a Win
q: Maintaining the energy and enthusiasm required to succeed long-term is exceedingly difficult when teams aren't putting points on the board.
Waiting until the external tide turns and/or the performance roadblocks dissipate is more hope than strategy.
They know a team that is struggling needs a win, no matter where it comes from.
Creating something significant from scratch is just the ticket for a team that needs to post a victory.
Charitable efforts are another great place for the team to score an easy win.
Nothing feels better to a team that hasn't had a victory lately.

t: Should Teachers Show Examples of Their Own Work to Students
q: One side says only put up the examples that other students have done or just the mere basics so that students won't take one look at a project and give up because they can't fathom being able to compare to what they see.
Spoiler alert: I answer with an emphatic YES. However, certain conditions must be cultivated for this method not to backfire.

But when a student fancies themselves a student artist and then discerns at the completion of a project that their piece is inferior to many of their peers, this can be quite rattling. It can act just like a ravenous beast, devouring the student's sense of self as an artist.
The solution to this is crafting a class culture where art is an infinite game of personal improvement versus a finite game of competition.

It's very powerful to create work in front of students — not at length, as this can be boring, but for 3-4 minute intervals, talking through as you work the barriers you're having to overcome, the decisions you're making.

It sends an "ooh ah wow" signal of Credibility (the most foundational of the Five Key Beliefs). It makes clear the unclear (this is critical for the Effort and Efficacy beliefs, especially for secondary students).

t: Problems That Arise Gradually or How to Boil a Frog
q: Yet, many problems go unaddressed by leaders until just before the volcano is ready to blow.
The frog becomes unwittingly complacent before it realizes the magnitude of the problem. By then, it is too late.
Threats and problems that arise gradually rather than suddenly are commonly missed by even the smartest of leaders.
The negative effects of a problem can mushroom slowly without warning or notice, especially for leaders busy with issues they know they must address.
If you realize gradualism has been dulling your senses, give the problem the focus it deserves.
Some colleagues think so highly of themselves that it's a wonder their feet stay on the ground.
Prima Donna is a derogatory term that originates from the Italian Opera.
Because they believe they are the star of the show and invaluable, Prima Donnas don't take feedback well.
It is better to tolerate the Prima Donna than to suffer through their bad-tempered reactions to criticism or to lose them.
Prima Donnas become who they are precisely because others fear the backlash of telling them the truth.
Good leaders don't protect anyone from feedback and constructive criticism.
